HIAI019

TrianglesCirclesGeometry
Game: Three equilateral triangles sit on the sides of a triangle, and a point travels from circle to circle around them.
How to play: Drag a corner dot or a dot on a circle, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the 60° marks, or press Reset for a fresh picture.
Look for the math

The picture looks like a tangle of circles, but a point started on one of them makes a complete lap and lands exactly where it began. The lap also draws a new equilateral triangle. This is a problem of Hirotaka Ebisui, reported on the original cut-the-knot page. That page today shows a GeoGebra figure instead of the Java applet; the applet was checked in a 2012 Wayback capture, which embeds code="HIAI019" with ShowNames=1.

Three sides, three equilateral triangles

On each side of triangle ABC we put an equilateral triangle: ABC′, BCA′ and CAB′. Each has a circumcircle. These are Napoleon triangles: by Napoleon's theorem their centres form an equilateral triangle, and the three circumcircles all pass through one common point. For an acute triangle that meeting point is a Fermat point: the checks find its three viewing angles are either 120°, 120°, 120° or 60°, 60°, 120°, depending on which of the two Fermat points the construction reaches.

A lap around the circles

Start at D on the circle over AB. Join D to B (the vertex shared by the first two circles) and extend the line to its other crossing with the next circle: call it E. Join E to C and extend to F on the third circle; join F to A and extend back to the first circle. The porism says the last point is D again. The check follows this lap for thousands of triangles and starting angles: the largest return error was under 0.0001 board units on a 400-by-250 board.

Why DEF is equilateral

The angle at the extra vertex C′ is 60° because ABC′ is equilateral. Angles ADB and AC′B stand on the same chord AB of the same circle, so by the inscribed angle theorem they are equal or add to 180°: D sees AB under 60° or 120°. The same holds at E and F, and the chain's three sides then meet at 60° each. The checks confirm both the 60-or-120 claim at the chain points and the three 60° angles of DEF; the measured sides agree to better than 0.0001 units.

One quirk in the old code

The applet's circle-line cut refuses a line whose horizontal and vertical steps are both at most one pixel, and its catch simply leaves the point unmoved. In that rare, nearly horizontal case the chain is not completed, so the theorem is checked only on pictures with clean cuts. The other harmless quirk is kept: Reset picks a random starting angle but the first lap immediately replaces it. Keyboard buttons for moving D, E and F are an accessibility addition; the rules and geometry are the applet's.

Try this: press Reset a few times, then tick statement to see the 60° marks at D, E and F. Move D a long way round its circle and watch the marks stay at 60°.
